theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Before assembling a fabricated frame, what should you check first?
options: The paint colour the customer would like
How long the welding cables will reach
The drawing and that every part is there
The weather forecast for the coming week

questions.stem: Why are parts marked with a number or letter before assembly?
options: So the parts weigh a little less when lifted
So each part goes in the right place
So the primer and paint stick better later
So each welder can sign the parts they made

questions.stem: What is an assembly sequence?
options: The list of prices paid for each part
The number of welders who work on the job
The time by which the whole job must be done
The order in which parts are fitted and joined

questions.stem: Why is a flat, level work surface (setting-out table) used for assembling a frame?
options: So the frame can be painted while it is built
So sparks cannot reach the workshop floor
So the frame is built flat, with no twist
So the frame cools down faster after welding

questions.stem: Which tool is best for holding two flat bars tightly together while they are tack welded?
options: A G-clamp or F-clamp
A centre punch and hammer
A long steel tape measure
A spirit level on top

questions.stem: What are locking pliers used for in fabrication?
options: Cutting through thick steel bar
Holding parts in place while fitting
Measuring the angle of a joint
Bending pipe to a set shape and size

questions.stem: What is a jig?
options: A small hammer used for tapping parts into line
A special electrode for welding thin steel
A gauge used to measure the thickness of plate
A holder that sets each part in place

questions.stem: Why should clamps be placed where they do not get in the way of the weld?
options: So the clamps are easier to paint later
So the joint can be welded without stopping
So the clamps get hot and grip harder
So the frame weighs less when it is lifted

questions.stem: How can you check that a rectangular frame is square?
options: Measure one long side and one short side
Stand back and check it carefully by eye
Check that the two diagonals are equal
Weigh each corner with a spring scale

questions.stem: A frame's diagonals measure 1 502 mm and 1 510 mm. What does this tell you?
options: The frame is out of square
The frame is square and ready to weld
The frame is level from end to end
The frame is the right height and width

questions.stem: Using the 3-4-5 rule, which measurements show a right angle (90°) at a corner?
options: Sides of 600 mm and 600 mm, and 600 mm across
Sides of 600 mm and 800 mm, and 1 400 mm across
Sides of 500 mm and 800 mm, and 1 000 mm across
Sides of 600 mm and 800 mm, and 1 000 mm across

questions.stem: Which tool checks that a post is upright (vertical)?
options: A bevel gauge set at 45°
A long steel tape measure
A spirit level or plumb line
A sharp scriber and rule

questions.stem: Why should measurements be taken from one datum (starting) edge?
options: So fewer measuring tools are needed
So small errors do not add up along the job
So the job is quicker to paint at the end
So the tape measure lasts longer

questions.stem: Two parts do not line up by 3 mm. What should you do?
options: Find out why, then adjust or re-cut so they fit
Force them with a sledge hammer until they meet
Fill the gap with extra weld metal
Leave it, as 3 mm will not matter

questions.stem: What is a packer or shim used for in assembly?
options: To cut a part down to its length
To clean the slag off the weld
To test how strong a bolt is in use
To fill a small gap and set height

questions.stem: What is a podger (drift) used for when bolting steel?
options: Tightening nuts to the right torque
Lining up the bolt holes in two parts
Cutting new threads on to a bolt
Measuring how long the bolt is

questions.stem: Why is a frame tacked at each corner first, then checked, before full welding?
options: So errors can be fixed before full welding
So fewer electrodes or less gas are used
So the paint can go on that much sooner
So the frame ends up a bit lighter

questions.stem: Tack welds on opposite corners of a frame are made in a balanced order. Why?
options: To make the job look neater to the client
To use up the short electrode stubs
To spread the heat and reduce distortion
So the welder has less walking to do

questions.stem: A tack weld cracks while the frame is being checked. What should you do?
options: Weld straight over it
Leave it, as the full weld will fix it
Hit it with a hammer to close the crack
Grind it out and re-tack it

questions.stem: Which welding order helps keep a long joint straight?
options: One long, slow run from one end to the other
Back-step or skip welding in short runs
Welding only one side of the job
Using the highest current possible

questions.stem: A tacked frame is out of square. What is the right way to correct it?
options: Weld it up fully, then hammer it square
Leave it, as the paint will hide the error
Break a tack, square it, then re-tack
Add extra tacks along the long side

questions.stem: Why is a washer placed under a nut?
options: To spread the load and protect the surface
To make the bolt a little longer
To stop the bolt from being tightened too far
To act as a spacer for tack welding

questions.stem: What is a spring washer or a nylon-insert lock nut for?
options: To make the nut easier to take off later
To seal the bolt against rain water
To insulate the bolt from electricity
To stop the nut shaking loose

questions.stem: When choosing the length of a bolt, what should you aim for?
options: The nut reaching only half way on the thread
At least 50 mm sticking out past the nut
A thread or two showing past the nut
The nut only half on, to save time

questions.stem: What is a blind (pop) rivet useful for?
options: Joining thick plate that carries heavy loads
Joining sheet when you can only reach one side
Lifting heavy parts with a crane hook
Lining up bolt holes before bolting

questions.stem: What size hole is drilled for a blind rivet?
options: A little larger than the rivet, as the maker says
Half the size of the rivet body
Twice the size of the rivet body
Any size at all, as the rivet swells to fill the hole

questions.stem: Why should the bolts in a flange or base plate be tightened in a criss-cross order?
options: So the bolts can be undone faster
So that fewer spanners are needed
So the threads do not show past the nut
So the parts pull together evenly

questions.stem: Which tool tightens a bolt to a set tightness (torque)?
options: A pipe wrench
A torque wrench
A pair of pliers
A cold chisel

questions.stem: Why is a centre punch mark made before drilling a hole?
options: To make the finished hole a little bigger
To harden the metal round the hole
To stop the drill wandering off the mark
To keep the drill bit cool as it cuts

questions.stem: When drilling a part on a pedestal drill, how should it be held?
options: Held firmly in your hand, with a good grip
Held in gloved hands near the bit
Held by a helper's fingers on top
Clamped in a machine vice or to the table

questions.stem: How should a heavy fabricated frame be moved at the Centre?
options: With enough people or a lifting aid
By one strong person, as fast as possible
By dragging it along the floor by one leg
By flipping it end over end across the floor

questions.stem: Why should fingers be kept clear of the joint when two heavy parts are being brought together?
options: The parts get too hot to hold
Parts can slip and trap or crush fingers
Fingers leave grease on the part
It makes the holes wear out

questions.stem: Which PPE is most important when grinding welds flush on an assembly?
options: A peaked cap and dark sunglasses
A cotton dust coat and nothing else
Face shield, glasses, gloves and ear muffs
A welding helmet with the filter down

questions.stem: When the assembly is finished, what is it checked against?
options: The drawing: sizes, squareness and details
A similar job made by another trainee
What the materials cost to buy at the store
How long it took to make

questions.stem: What is a tolerance on a drawing?
options: The total weight of the finished part
The number of parts needed for the job
How long the paint should last outdoors
How far a size may vary and still pass

questions.stem: A gate frame is finished, but one bar is 10 mm out of place. The tolerance is ±2 mm. What should you do?
options: Send it out, as it is close enough
Report it and correct it before it leaves
Hide it with a thick coat of paint
Bend the bar with a hammer when no one is looking

questions.stem: Why are sharp edges and spatter removed from a finished assembly?
options: So it weighs a little more when sold
So it looks old and worn
So it is safe to handle and paint
So the welds are fully hidden

questions.stem: Before painting a steel frame, what should be done?
options: Clean off rust, grease and slag first
Paint straight over the slag and spatter
Wet it all over with water first
Leave it out in the sun for a week

questions.stem: Why are the welds on a handrail often ground smooth?
options: To make the welds a lot stronger in use
To use up old grinding discs
So the rail is lighter to carry
So hands are not cut or snagged on it

questions.stem: Delroy is making burglar bars for a window in Mandeville. What must he check on site before he builds them?
options: The colour of the walls round the window
The exact sizes of the window opening
The name of the street outside
How high the roof of the house is

questions.stem: At the end of assembly work, what should be done with clamps and tools?
options: Clean, check and put them away
Leave them on the frame for the next class
Throw them in a box along with the scrap
Leave them on the floor under the bench

questions.stem: Why should a finished job be recorded on the job card?
options: So the same job can be sold twice
So no one else ever needs to check it
To record what was done and checked
To fill the job card up with writing

questions.stem: Two trainees are lifting a frame into place. How should they work?
options: Each lifts as soon as he or she is ready
Agree the plan; one person calls the lift
One lifts while the other only watches
Both shout orders at the same time

questions.stem: Why is a gap sometimes left between parts in a fabricated joint before welding?
options: So the joint is lighter
To save on filler metal
So the parts can move during welding
So the weld can penetrate fully

questions.stem: A stainless steel bolt is used to join aluminium sheet outdoors. How can galvanic corrosion be prevented?
options: Fit insulating washers between them
Paint the bolt bright red first
Use a much longer and thicker bolt
Tighten the nut up extra hard

essays.stem: Describe how you would plan the assembly of a fabricated item, such as a steel table frame, from reading the drawing to setting out the parts.
essays.modelAnswer: First read the assembly drawing and the parts list, and check the sizes, angles, joint types, weld symbols and tolerances. Ask the instructor about anything that is not clear. Check every part against the list: count the parts, measure them, check that they are square and deburred, and mark each one with its part number. Plan the assembly order: which parts go together first, where the tacks go, which joints are welded or bolted, and how distortion will be controlled. Decide which tools and holding devices are needed, such as clamps, magnetic squares, a jig and packers. Prepare a clean, flat, level setting-out table. Mark the main lines or the outline of the frame on the table with chalk or soapstone, and set out the parts on it in position, ready for clamping and tacking.
markingPoints: Reads the drawing and parts list for sizes, joints and tolerances, and asks about anything unclear
Checks, measures and marks every part
Plans the assembly order, tacking and distortion control
Chooses the tools and holding devices needed
Prepares a flat setting-out table and sets out the parts

essays.stem: Explain how clamps, jigs, magnetic squares and a setting-out table help when assembling fabricated components, and how to use them safely.
essays.modelAnswer: A flat, level setting-out table gives a true surface to build on, so the frame comes out flat and free of twist, and lines can be marked on it. Clamps, such as G-clamps, F-clamps and locking pliers, hold parts tightly in position so that they do not move while they are measured and tacked. Magnetic squares hold steel parts at 90° or 45° and free the hands for tacking. A jig holds parts in the same position every time, so that many identical items can be made quickly and accurately. To use them safely, choose a clamp of the right size, place it so that it does not get in the way of the weld, and tighten it firmly but not so hard that it bends the part. Keep fingers out of pinch points. Clamps and magnets get hot near the weld, strong magnets can trap fingers, and welding close to a magnet can make the arc wander.
markingPoints: Setting-out table gives a flat, true surface and a place to mark lines
Clamps hold parts still while they are measured and tacked
Magnetic squares hold parts at set angles and free the hands
Jigs give the same position every time for repeat parts
Safe use: right size, clear of the weld, not overtightened, fingers clear, hot near the weld

essays.stem: Explain how you check that a rectangular frame is square, flat and the right size during assembly. Use an example with numbers.
essays.modelAnswer: First measure the length and width of the frame from the datum edges and compare them with the drawing and its tolerance. Then measure the two diagonals, from corner to corner. If the frame is square, the two diagonals are equal. For example, a frame 1 200 mm by 1 600 mm should have diagonals of 2 000 mm each, because it is a 3-4-5 triangle made 400 times bigger. If one diagonal reads 2 004 mm and the other 1 996 mm, the frame is out of square, so push in on the corners of the long diagonal until both read the same. To check that it is flat, lay it on the setting-out table and look for a corner that rocks or lifts, or use a straight edge and a spirit level. Check again after tacking and after welding, because welding can pull the frame out of shape.
markingPoints: Measures length and width against the drawing and tolerance
Measures both diagonals; equal diagonals mean the frame is square
Gives a correct worked example with numbers
Explains how to correct a frame that is out of square
Checks flatness, and checks again after tacking and welding

essays.stem: Explain how you would tack and weld a rectangular frame so that distortion is kept as small as possible.
essays.modelAnswer: Clamp the parts to the flat table in their right positions. Put a small tack at each corner, working in a balanced order, for example one corner and then the opposite corner, and on both sides of a joint where possible. Check the sizes, the diagonals and the flatness after tacking, and correct anything that is out before welding. Then weld in a balanced order: weld short runs on opposite corners in turn rather than finishing one corner at a time, and use back-step or skip welding on long joints so that the heat is spread out. Keep the frame clamped down while welding, and let it cool between runs if it gets very hot. Use the right current and do not make welds bigger than needed, because more weld metal means more shrinkage. Check the frame again after welding, both while it is clamped and after it is released.
markingPoints: Clamps the parts and tacks the corners in a balanced order
Checks size, diagonals and flatness, and corrects before welding
Welds in a balanced order, with short, back-step or skip runs
Keeps the frame clamped, lets it cool, and avoids oversized welds
Checks the frame again after welding

essays.stem: Describe how to make a bolted joint between two steel parts, from marking out to tightening.
essays.modelAnswer: Mark the hole centres on the first part from the drawing, using a rule, square and scriber, and centre punch each one. Clamp the part in a machine vice or to the drill table. Drill a small pilot hole, then open it out to the clearance size for the bolt, a little larger than the bolt. Deburr the holes. Clamp the two parts together in their right positions and either mark through the holes onto the second part or drill both together. Line up the holes with a podger if needed, keeping fingers clear. Fit the bolts with a washer under the nut, and a spring washer or lock nut where there is vibration. Tighten by hand first, then tighten the nuts in a criss-cross order to the tightness the drawing gives, using a torque wrench if one is needed. Check that a thread or two shows past each nut.
markingPoints: Marks and centre punches the hole positions from the drawing
Clamps the work, drills a pilot then the clearance size, and deburrs
Lines up the parts and holes safely, with a podger if needed
Fits washers, and locking washers or nuts where there is vibration
Tightens in a criss-cross order to the set torque; a thread or two past the nut

essays.stem: Explain how to join two pieces of sheet with blind (pop) rivets, and say when rivets are a better choice than welding.
essays.modelAnswer: Choose the rivet type, diameter and length from the maker's chart to suit the total thickness of the sheets being joined (the grip). Mark the rivet positions in a straight line, evenly spaced as the drawing shows, keeping each rivet well in from the edge; a common guide is at least twice the rivet diameter. Clamp the sheets together and drill the first hole to the size the rivet maker gives, just larger than the rivet. Fit a rivet or a temporary fastener to hold the sheets, then drill and fit the rest. Push each rivet through, put the rivet tool over the stem and squeeze until the stem snaps off. Check that each rivet head sits flat and tight. Rivets are better than welding for thin sheet that would distort or burn through, for joining different metals such as aluminium to steel, for painted or galvanised sheet, and where you can only reach one side.
markingPoints: Chooses the rivet from the maker's chart to suit the grip
Marks positions evenly spaced and well in from the edge
Clamps the sheets and drills holes to the maker's size, holding as it goes
Sets each rivet until the stem snaps, and checks it sits flat and tight
Gives sound reasons when rivets are better than welding

essays.stem: Describe how a finished fabricated assembly is inspected, and what you should do if part of it is outside the tolerance.
essays.modelAnswer: Inspect the assembly against the drawing. Measure the overall sizes and the position of each part with a tape or rule, and compare them with the drawing sizes and tolerances. Check squareness by measuring the diagonals or using a square, check flatness on the table or with a straight edge, and check that uprights are plumb with a spirit level. Count the parts and fasteners to make sure nothing is missing. Look at every weld for size, cracks, porosity, undercut and spatter, and check that bolts are tight and rivets are set. Check the finish: no sharp edges, burrs or slag. If something is outside the tolerance, do not hide it or send it out. Mark it, tell the instructor and agree the fix, such as re-setting a part or making a new one. After it is fixed, check it again and record the result on the job card.
markingPoints: Measures sizes and positions against the drawing and tolerance
Checks square, flat and plumb
Checks parts, fasteners and welds
Checks the finish for sharp edges, burrs and slag
Out of tolerance: marks it, reports it, agrees the fix, re-checks and records

essays.stem: Describe the main hazards when assembling fabricated components, and how each one is controlled.
essays.modelAnswer: Manual handling: steel parts and frames are heavy and awkward and can cause back injuries and crushed feet. Plan the lift, use enough people or a lifting aid, lift with the legs and wear safety boots. Pinch and crush points: fingers can be trapped between parts, in clamps or under magnets. Keep fingers clear when parts are brought together, and use a tool such as a podger, not fingers, to line up holes. Sharp edges and burrs: wear gloves and deburr parts early. Hot work: tacking and welding cause burns, arc flash, fumes and fire, so wear full welding PPE, use screens, ventilate the area and clear burnables. Grinding: sparks and broken discs can fly, so wear a face shield over glasses, gloves and hearing protection, and check the disc and guard. Trips: keep cables, hoses and offcuts off the floor. Follow the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Manual handling and its controls
Pinch and crush points and their controls
Sharp edges and burrs and their controls
Hot work hazards and their controls
Grinding and trip hazards and their controls

essays.stem: Explain how to finish a fabricated assembly ready to hand over to a customer.
essays.modelAnswer: When the assembly has passed inspection, remove all slag and spatter with a chipping hammer and wire brush. Grind welds smooth where hands will touch them, such as on handrails and gates, and blend them into the parent metal without cutting into it. File or grind off all burrs and sharp edges, and round off sharp corners. Clean off rust, grease, oil and marking with a degreaser or wire brush, so that the paint will stick. Put a primer on bare steel as soon as possible, because steel soon rusts in Jamaica's damp, salty air, then the top coat or other finish the job sheet asks for. Check that moving parts such as hinges and latches work freely, and fit any loose parts. Label the job, record it on the job card and protect it so that it is not damaged before handover.
markingPoints: Removes slag and spatter
Grinds welds smooth where needed and removes burrs and sharp edges
Cleans off rust, grease and marking before painting
Primes bare steel quickly and applies the finish asked for
Checks moving parts, labels, records and protects the job

essays.stem: Explain why good communication and records matter when a team assembles a fabricated job. Give examples.
essays.modelAnswer: In an assembly team, several people work on the same job, often at the same time. If they do not talk clearly, mistakes happen: two people may cut the same part, a part may be fitted the wrong way round, or someone may start welding while another is still checking the frame. Before starting, the team should agree the plan, who does each task and the order of work. When lifting, one person should call the lift so that everyone moves together. Measurements and checks should be called out and written down, for example 'diagonals 1 500 mm and 1 502 mm'. Problems such as a part out of tolerance or a faulty clamp must be reported to the instructor at once. Records such as the job card, the ticked parts list and the inspection sheet show what was done, by whom and what was checked. They help the next shift, prove the job meets the drawing, and help find the cause if a problem comes up later.
markingPoints: Explains the mistakes poor communication causes, with an example
Plan, tasks and order agreed before starting
One person calls the lift; measurements called out and written down
Problems reported to the instructor at once
Records kept and why they matter

practical1.title: Assembling and welding a rectangular steel frame from pre-cut parts
practical1.brief: As a group, assemble a rectangular frame, about 900 mm × 600 mm, from pre-cut 25 mm square tube (four sides and one centre rail), following the assembly drawing. Check and mark every part against the parts list, set out the frame on the setting-out table, clamp it and tack it in a balanced order. Check the sizes and diagonals and correct the frame before it is welded, then weld it in a balanced order and check it again. Share the work so that every member checks parts, sets up at least one corner with a clamp or magnetic square, makes at least two tacks, and takes and records one set of checks while the assessor watches. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the frame is finished and the area is clean.
materials: 25 mm × 25 mm × 2 mm mild steel square tube, pre-cut to the parts list (4 sides and 1 centre rail)
Setting-out table, G-clamps, F-clamps, locking pliers and magnetic squares
Tape measure, steel rule, engineer's square and soapstone
MMAW machine with 2.5 mm electrodes, or the Centre's usual process for thin tube
Angle grinder, files, chipping hammer and wire brush
photos: Parts laid out, checked and marked against the parts list
The frame set out and clamped on the table, with magnetic squares at the corners
A tape across the diagonals after tacking, with the readings written down
The frame being welded in a balanced order
The finished frame with the final diagonal check
The area cleaned, with tools put away
checklist: Wore suitable PPE throughout, including full welding PPE for tacking and welding
Checked and marked parts against the parts list and drawing
Set out and clamped a corner square, with the clamps clear of the weld
Made small, well-fused tacks in a balanced order
Measured and recorded sizes and diagonals, and helped correct the frame before welding
Finished frame within ±2 mm on size, diagonals within 3 mm of each other, and flat on the table
Left the area safe and tidy, with tools cleaned and put away
safety: Lift and move the frame with two or more people, and lift with your legs
Keep fingers clear of pinch points between parts, clamps and magnets
Tack and weld only in a screened area, with ventilation and burnables cleared
Treat tacked and welded parts as hot: use pliers or gloves and mark hot work
Wear a face shield over safety glasses when grinding, and check the disc and guard

practical2.title: Assembling a bolted and riveted wall shelf
practical2.brief: As a group, assemble a wall shelf from the drawing: two brackets, each made from 40 mm × 40 mm × 5 mm angle and 40 mm × 6 mm flat bar bolted together with M10 bolts, and a shelf of 1.2 mm mild steel sheet fixed to the brackets with blind rivets. Each member marks out and centre punches at least two holes, drills them on the pedestal drill (pilot hole first) with the work clamped, deburrs them, fits and tightens at least one bolt, and sets at least two rivets while the assessor watches. The group then checks the assembly against the drawing for size, square and level. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the assembly is checked and the area is clean.
materials: 40 mm × 40 mm × 5 mm mild steel angle and 40 mm × 6 mm flat bar, cut to the drawing
1.2 mm mild steel sheet for the shelf, cut to size
M10 bolts, nuts, flat washers and spring washers
Blind rivets and a rivet tool, with drills of the size the rivet maker gives
Pedestal drill with a machine vice, drills, centre punch, scriber, square and rule
Spanners, a torque wrench if available, files and a spirit level
photos: Parts marked out, with the hole centres punched
Work clamped in the machine vice on the pedestal drill
A bracket bolted up, showing the washers and the thread past the nut
Rivets being set in the shelf
The finished assembly with a square and a spirit level on it
The drill and bench cleaned, with the swarf brushed up
checklist: Wore safety glasses, with hair and sleeves secured and no gloves at the drill
Marked out and centre punched hole positions accurately from the drawing
Clamped the work and drilled a pilot hole, then the full size, at a suitable speed
Deburred the holes and lined up the parts with a podger, keeping fingers clear
Fitted washers and tightened bolts in a criss-cross order, with a thread or two showing
Set rivets that sit flat and tight in holes of the right size
Assembly within ±2 mm of the drawing, square and level
Left the drill and bench clean, with swarf brushed up and not cleared by hand
safety: Always clamp the work at the drill; never hold it by hand
No gloves, loose sleeves or rings at the pedestal drill; tie back long hair
Use the drill guard, and take the chuck key out before starting the drill
Clear swarf with a brush after the drill has stopped, never with your fingers
Keep fingers clear of pinch points when lining up holes and setting rivets
